category.text: $course$/Game Theory/Chapter 10 - Bargaining, Coalitions and the Shapley Value (Quiz)

name.text: C10 Q1 - Nash bargaining with an outside option

questiontext.text: Two parties divide 100. Party 1's disagreement payoff is 20 and party 2's is 0; utilities are linear in money. Under the Nash bargaining solution, how much does party 1 receive?

generalfeedback.text: Maximise \((x-20)(100-x)\). The first-order condition \(120 - 2x = 0\) gives \(x = 60\). The rule is: guarantee each party its disagreement payoff, then split the remaining surplus of 80 evenly, giving 20 + 40 = 60.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not one of Nash's four bargaining axioms?

generalfeedback.text: Nash's axioms are Pareto efficiency, symmetry, invariance to affine transformations of utility, and independence of irrelevant alternatives. Envy-freeness belongs to fair-division theory and plays no role here.

feedback.text: It is one of the four, and the most debated.

questiontext.text: In Rubinstein's alternating-offers game over a pie of size 1 with common discount factor \(\delta = 0.5\), what share does the first proposer receive in the unique subgame perfect equilibrium? Give a decimal to two places.

generalfeedback.text: The proposer receives \(\dfrac{1}{1+\delta} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} \approx 0.67\). Impatience is costly, so the ability to move first is worth more when players are impatient. As \(\delta \to 1\) the shares converge to 0.5 each, matching the Nash bargaining solution.

questiontext.text: An allocation is in the core of a coalitional game when:

generalfeedback.text: Core membership means the whole value is distributed and no coalition, however small, could guarantee its own members more by leaving. It is a stability condition against group deviations, in contrast with Nash equilibrium's unilateral deviations.

answer.text: It distributes the full value of the grand coalition and no coalition can guarantee its members more by breaking away
Every player receives the same amount

feedback.text: That is equal division, not the core.

answer.text: It maximises the sum of payoffs

feedback.text: Efficiency is only one of the core's conditions.
The Shapley value can lie outside the core.

questiontext.text: Three players have \(v(\emptyset) = v(1) = v(2) = v(3) = 0\), \(v(12) = 90\), \(v(13) = 80\), \(v(23) = 70\) and \(v(123) = 120\). What is player 1's Shapley value?

generalfeedback.text: Player 1's marginal contributions across the six orderings are \(0, 0, 90, 50, 80, 50\); their average is \(\phi_1 = 270/6 = 45\). Players 2 and 3 receive 40 and 35, and the three shares sum to 120 as efficiency requires.

questiontext.text: Using the same characteristic function, what is player 3's Shapley value?

generalfeedback.text: Player 3's marginal contributions are \(30, 80, 30, 70, 0, 0\), averaging \(\phi_3 = 210/6 = 35\). Player 3 is the weakest partner - the pair (2,3) creates the least value - and receives the smallest share.

name.text: C10 Q7 - Shapley and the core

questiontext.text: The Shapley value always lies inside the core when the core is non-empty.

generalfeedback.text: False. In the three-firm example the core is the single point \((50, 40, 30)\) while the Shapley value is \((45, 40, 35)\). Players 1 and 2 would receive only 85 under Shapley yet can guarantee themselves 90 alone. Fairness axioms and stability against blocking are genuinely different requirements. (They do coincide in the special class of convex games.)

name.text: C10 Q8 - The null player axiom

questiontext.text: The Shapley value's null-player axiom says that:

generalfeedback.text: A player who adds nothing to any coalition - whose marginal contribution is zero everywhere - receives zero. This is the axiom that makes the Shapley value a meaningful attribution of credit, and it is why SHAP values in machine learning assign zero to a feature that never changes the prediction.

answer.text: A player whose marginal contribution to every coalition is zero receives a payoff of zero
A player who acts alone receives zero

feedback.text: Singleton value is unrelated to the axiom.

answer.text: Every player must receive a strictly positive amount

feedback.text: The axiom says the opposite in the relevant case.
That is closer to the efficiency axiom.
